title: Emergency Medical Card
overflowHelp: Shorten the text in these sections. The text never shrinks to fit, so it stays easy to read.
missingHeading: The card's fonts cannot show these characters

fields.modeBilingualHelp: Both sides show the same information, each in a different language. Space is tighter, so keep text short.
fields.emblemHelp: The red cross is the symbol most people recognise for medical help. It is protected under the Geneva Conventions and, in India, the Geneva Conventions Act 1960. The Rod of Asclepius is not protected. You choose which to use.
fields.name: Full name
fields.birthYearHelp: Just the year. Anyone who finds your wallet can read this card.
fields.bloodGroupHelp: Optional. It goes next to your name. Hospitals always test before a transfusion, so this is for information only.
fields.showAddress: Print my address on the card
fields.conditionHelp: Use words a stranger will understand, like type 1 diabetes, epilepsy, or peanut allergy.
fields.iconHelp: Optional. Choose an icon, or upload an SVG or a PNG at least 600 pixels wide and 600 pixels tall. If you leave it, the card shows a stethoscope.
fields.doHelp: One instruction per line, up to 4. Write for someone who does not know your condition.
fields.doNotHelp: One per line, up to 4. Each line finishes the heading, so write "Give me insulin", not "Do not give me insulin".
fields.carriesHelp: Say what you carry and where. For example, glucose tablets in my left jacket pocket.
fields.allergiesHelp: One allergy on each line. If you leave it empty, the card says None known.
fields.qr: Add a QR code to the back of the card
fields.qrHelp: It goes at the top right of the back. Scanning it saves one contact with your emergency numbers and anything else you tick below.
fields.fontHelp: Changes the typeface for Latin, Greek, and Cyrillic text. Condensed typefaces fit more on the card. Other scripts use a font made for them.
fields.fontCustomHelp: Use a font installed on this computer, such as Helvetica. Choose the file, or pick from installed fonts if your browser allows it. The font is never uploaded.
fields.fontCustomNone: You have not chosen a font yet. The card uses the default typeface until you do.
fields.fontCustomNoBold: Using {name}. This font has no bold weight, so bold text uses the regular weight. Add a bold file if you have one.
fields.showAddressHelp: Off by default. Anyone who finds your wallet can read your address.
fields.prefillNote: This text is suggested for {condition}. It is based on {sources}. {review} It is general first aid guidance and is not advice about you. Check it with your doctor before you rely on it.
fields.prefillEdited: You have changed the suggested text. Check your wording with your doctor. This tool cannot check medical information and is not responsible for what is printed.
fields.iconSearch: Search icons, for example heart or brain
fields.iconPickerHelp: Icons are from Lucide. Medical icons are shown first. Use the search box to find others.
fields.qrIncludeCondition: Main condition, saved as the contact note
fields.qrIncludeAddress: Home address, saved as the contact address
fields.qrSizeHelp: Larger is easier to scan and uses more of the back.
fields.qrMeterText: {bytes} bytes. {modules} squares on each side, each {mm} mm wide.
fields.qrEasy: A phone can scan this easily.
fields.qrClose: A phone can scan this from close up. To be safe, remove some information or choose a larger size.
fields.qrDense: A phone cannot scan this reliably. Remove some information, shorten the address, or choose a larger size.
fields.qrNoNumbers: None of your emergency contacts has a phone number yet.
fields.countryKnown: This country's emergency number was checked on {date}. Check it's still right.
fields.countryUnknown: We do not have this country's emergency number yet. Type it in below.
fields.emergencyAmbulanceHelp: Fill this in only if it is different from the emergency number.
fields.instructionsNote: Check every instruction with your doctor before you print, especially any that mention a medicine or a dose.
fields.medicinesNote: Use the names on your prescription. When your medicines change, print a new card. An out-of-date list can lead to the wrong treatment.
fields.symbolsHelp: Symbols from Wikimedia Commons. Hover over one to see who made it and its licence.
fields.labelsFallback: The card's headings, such as DO and DO NOT, are not translated into {languages} yet, so they will print in English. Everything you type is printed as you type it. You can help translate the headings on GitHub.
fields.labelsUnreviewed: The card's headings in {languages} were translated with AI and have not been checked by a native speaker yet. Read them on the preview. If something is wrong, you can help fix it on GitHub.
fields.showDate: Print the month you last updated the card
fields.showDateHelp: It goes in the bottom corner of the back and takes no room. Whoever reads the card can see how recent your medicines list is.
fields.phoneInvalid: This does not look like a phone number. Use digits, like {example}.
fields.birthYearInvalid: Enter the year as four digits, like 1958.
fields.phoneAbroad: If you travel abroad, add the country code at the start, like {calling}.

seoTitle: Emergency Medical Card · Free medical ID wallet card maker
seoDescription: Make a free medical ID wallet card with your condition, what to do, your medicines, and who to call. Nothing you type leaves your browser.
faqIntro: There's more detail on the privacy and terms pages.

faq.q: What is an emergency medical card?
faq.a: An emergency medical card, also called a medical ID card, is a small card you carry that tells a stranger how to help you when you can't tell them yourself. It says what your condition is, what to do and what not to do, which medicines you take, what you're allergic to, and who to call.

faq.q: What else are these cards called?
faq.a: People call it a medical ID card, a medical alert card, a medical wallet card, an emergency information card, or an ICE card, where ICE stands for In Case of Emergency. People with one condition often name it after that condition, like a diabetic card, an epilepsy card, or an allergy card.

Anyone who might need a stranger to act quickly. That includes people with diabetes, epilepsy, a heart condition, a severe allergy, Addison's disease, dementia, or autism, and anyone who takes blood thinners. It's also worth having if you live alone, look after someone, or have a child with a condition who goes to school, camp, or a club without you.

Whenever you're away from the people who know you. Travelling abroad is the big one. Pick the local language as the second language in the Language menu, and the back of the card is printed in it for a stranger there to read. It also helps on a commute, on a run or a hike, at the gym, and on a night out. A card in your wallet still works when your phone is locked, flat, or broken.
Put it next to your ID or bank card, as that's where someone looks when they need to know who you are. Keep a second one in your bag or glovebox, and set the lock screen image on your phone.
Yes. There's nothing to pay, no account, and no adverts. The code is open source under the MIT licence.
Nowhere. Everything you type stays in your browser on your own device and is never sent to a server. To keep your card safe or move it to another device, choose Save a copy from the File menu.

faq.q: How do I print my wallet card?
faq.a: For a print shop, choose PDF for a print shop from the Download menu. The file is the card's exact size, and every letter in it is drawn as a shape, so it prints the same on any printer. Ask the shop to print it at 100% scale on thick card or PVC and to laminate it. If the shop asks for a different file, the same menu has a PNG of each side at 600 or 300 dpi, and an SVG. To print it yourself, choose Print at home. It puts the front and back side by side on an A4 or Letter page. Print that at actual size, cut the card out, fold it along the middle, and laminate it.

faq.q: Can I put the card on my phone?
faq.a: Yes. Choose Phone above the preview to see it, then choose Lock screen image from the Download menu. It's the same card laid out for a phone screen, placed below where the clock sits. Set it as your lock screen wallpaper and anyone can see it without unlocking your phone. Fill in your phone's own Medical ID or emergency information too.

faq.q: Is it the same as a medical ID bracelet?
faq.a: No, and they work well together. A bracelet is quicker to spot and survives water, but it only holds a few words. A card holds what to do, what not to do, your medicines, and your contacts. Plenty of people wear a bracelet that says "See wallet card".

faq.q: Is this the HSE medical card or the ABHA card?
faq.a: No. Ireland's medical card and India's ABHA health card are government health schemes. This is a card you carry so that strangers know how to help you in an emergency. It isn't linked to any government, insurer, or hospital.

faq.q: Can it be in my language?
faq.a: Probably. The card can be in one language, or two with one on each side, from 47 languages. You choose them in the Language menu. Indian languages, Thai, Khmer, Georgian, Armenian, Amharic, and every Latin, Greek, and Cyrillic language are set in a font made for them. The headings in languages other than English were translated with AI and haven't been checked by native speakers yet, and the editor tells you when that's the case. Arabic, Hebrew, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are coming later.

faq.q: Where does the suggested text come from?
faq.a: It was drafted with AI from public first aid pages by the NHS, Diabetes UK, Asthma + Lung UK, Epilepsy Action, and others, named beside each suggestion. A clinician hasn't reviewed it yet. Check it with your doctor before you print.

faq.q: How often should I update it?
faq.a: Whenever your medicines, your condition, or your contacts change. Turn on the date in the Look menu so whoever reads it can see how recent it is. If you save a copy from the File menu, you can open it later with Open a copy, change what's new, and download the card again.

You choose the size in the Size menu. The wallet card is 85.6 × 54 mm, the size of a bank card. The pocket card is 105 × 74 mm, the size of an A7 sheet, and has bigger text. There's also a lock screen image for your phone.

faq.q: What does the QR code do?
faq.a: When someone scans it with their phone camera, it saves one contact with your emergency numbers. You can add your condition, blood group, hospital, and address. It's off until you turn it on in the QR code section of the form.
It's the symbol most people recognise for medical help. It's also a protected emblem under the Geneva Conventions, so the Look menu lets you pick the Rod of Asclepius or no emblem instead.
